_about: Hand-authored, deterministic fixture corpus for the scoring golden master.
NOTHING here is sampled from the production database and nothing is generated
at test time: every article carries the scoring model's recorded response, so
tests/test_scoring_golden_master.py never needs a model, a network socket, or
a live Readwise call.
Scoring arithmetic these fixtures were designed against (app/services/scorer.py
and app/services/scoring_strategy.py):
specificity  = STANDALONE_SCORES[standalone_passages]   none 0 / a_few 9 / several 17 / many 25
novelty      = 15*novel_framing + CONTENT_TYPE_SCORES[content_type]
original_analysis 10 / opinion_with_evidence 8 / informational_summary 3
/ product_review 2 / news_or_roundup 0            (capped at 25)
depth        = 12*author_conviction + 8*practitioner_voice + COMPLETENESS_SCORES[content_completeness]
complete 5 / appears_truncated 2 / summary_or_excerpt 0   (capped at 25)
actionability= 12*named_framework + APPLICABLE_SCORES[applicable_ideas]
broadly 13 / narrowly 7 / not_really 0
info_score   = (specificity + actionability) * 2         (v5-reweighted)
author_boost = ArticleScorer.AUTHOR_BOOST_THRESHOLDS, matched on the author's
lowercased+stripped name against the authors table
priority     = info_score + author_boost
skip         = info_score < 30
value tier   = info_score >= 60 high / >= 30 medium / else low
'total_override' pins an InfoScore total that the v5 reweight cannot produce.
(specificity + actionability) * 2 is always even, so info_score == 30.0 exactly
is unreachable through the categorical mapping; the nearest reachable values are
26 and 32. InfoScore.total_override is a production field (v3/v4 strategies set
it), so pinning it at the strategy seam is a legitimate way to park an article
exactly on the skip_recommended boundary.

document.title: The Compounding Interest of Small Interfaces
document.author: Unrecorded Author
document.content: Every interface you ship is a promise you keep paying for. The teams that move fastest after year three are not the ones that shipped the most surface area, they are the ones that shipped the least. A narrow interface is a loan you never have to service. This piece walks through three production systems where the narrow choice looked slower for two quarters and then compounded for a decade, and names the pattern the surface-area tax.

model_response.overall_assessment: A sharp, opinionated piece that names a reusable pattern and defends it with real systems.

document.title: Why Your Retro Keeps Producing the Same Three Action Items
document.author: Sixty Line Writer
document.content: A retrospective that produces the same three action items every sprint is not a broken meeting, it is a working instrument reporting a constraint nobody is allowed to touch. The ritual is fine. The authority is missing. Until the person who can change the constraint is in the room, the retro will keep faithfully measuring the same wall, and the team will keep reading that measurement as a personal failure rather than a structural one.

model_response.argument_reason: Clear position, argued rather than reported.
model_response.insight_reason: The diagnosis transfers to most recurring meetings.
model_response.overall_assessment: A clear opinion piece with a diagnosis that transfers well beyond retrospectives.

document.title: Notes on Reading Code You Did Not Write
document.author: Midfield Essayist
document.content:
Reading unfamiliar code is a skill nobody teaches and everybody grades you on. The trick is not to read it. Run it, break it, and read only the parts that scream.

Start from the loudest failure and walk outward. The call stack is a reading order somebody already computed for you, and it is almost always better than the table of contents you would have written.

model_response.argument_reason: Practitioner notes rather than a sustained argument.
model_response.insight_reason: The walk-outward-from-the-failure habit is directly usable.
model_response.overall_assessment: Short practitioner notes with one genuinely useful habit.

document.title: The Two-Week Rule for Deprecations
document.author: Boost Author Five
document.content: We deprecate on a two-week clock and we have never regretted it. Week one the old path logs loudly. Week two it errors in staging and warns in production. Then it is gone. The rule works because it is short enough that nobody schedules around it and long enough that nobody is surprised by it, and because the clock starts the day the replacement lands rather than the day somebody files the ticket.

model_response.surprise_reason: Argues short deprecation windows beat long ones.
model_response.argument_reason: First-person practice with a defended position.
model_response.insight_reason: The two-week rule is named but assumes their release cadence.
model_response.overall_assessment: A named, defensible practice from real operating experience.

document.title: What Ten Years of Incident Reviews Taught Us
document.author: Boost Author Ten
document.content: After a decade of incident reviews the pattern is embarrassingly stable: the outage is never the thing you wrote the runbook for, and the runbook is never the thing that saved you. What saved you was that somebody had read the code recently. We stopped writing runbooks for scenarios and started writing them for systems, and our time to recovery halved in a year without a single new tool.

model_response.argument_reason: Ten years of practice behind a clear claim.
model_response.overall_assessment: A decade of practice distilled into one transferable reframe.

document.title: An Anonymous Field Report from a Migration
document.content: The migration took eleven months and was scoped at four. Nothing about the estimate was dishonest; the estimate simply priced the work and not the coordination. Half of every week went to convincing four teams that a shared deadline was real. If you are scoping a migration, price the meetings. They are not overhead on the work, they are most of the work, and no amount of tooling collapses them.

model_response.surprise_reason: Reframes migration cost as coordination cost.
model_response.argument_reason: A field report with a defended conclusion.
model_response.insight_reason: Diagnostic rather than something a reader can apply directly.
model_response.overall_assessment: A candid field report that reframes migration cost as coordination cost.

rescore_document.title: Attention Is a Budget, Not a Resource
rescore_document.author: Stub Source
rescore_document.content: Attention is a budget, not a resource, and the difference decides how you plan your week. A resource is depleted by use and restored by rest. A budget is allocated in advance and overspent silently. Teams that treat focus as a resource schedule recovery. Teams that treat it as a budget schedule the spending, which is the only one of the two that changes what actually gets built this quarter.

document.title: Estimates Are Predictions About Other People
document.author: Boost Author Seven
document.content: An estimate is not a prediction about the work, it is a prediction about the people who will interrupt the work. That is why estimates from the same engineer vary by a factor of three across two teams with identical codebases. If you want better estimates, do not buy a better estimation technique. Reduce the number of people who can interrupt, and the numbers converge on their own within about a quarter.

document.title: Against Dashboards
document.author: Barely Highlighted
document.content: A dashboard is a question you got tired of asking. That is fine for questions with stable answers and disastrous for everything else, because the dashboard outlives the question and nobody remembers what it was for. We deleted eleven of our fourteen dashboards and replaced them with three alerts and a weekly query somebody actually has to run by hand, and we caught more real problems in the following quarter than in the year before.

document.title: The Meeting That Should Have Been a Decision
document.author: PROLIFIC highlighter
document.content: Most meetings that should have been an email should actually have been a decision. The email is a symptom; the missing decision is the disease. When nobody is willing to own the call, the calendar fills with rehearsals of the call, and each rehearsal produces a document that argues for one more rehearsal. Name the decider before you name the agenda and half the recurring invitations dissolve on their own.

model_response.insight_reason: Useful mainly to whoever can appoint a decider.
